violation: No three-layer separation: no mutable AgentLocator (node_id, pid_ns_inode, node_pid, start_epoch) in gossip, and no Ed25519 CapabilityToken (rights bitmap, TTL) separate from identity

exit: RESOLVED 2026-08-02. The silo's oldest entry (opened 07-22), and the handoff predicted 'a design cycle on the scale of GOBLIN-DIV-047'. That was an OVERESTIMATE of the kind an-entry-predicts-its-own-cost warns about: the three-layer split shipped on 07-28 and the reopening was about WIRING, not design. What the entry did not predict is that two of the four pieces were wrong rather than merely absent. (1) REVOCATION WAS CHECKED WHERE IT COULD NOT MATTER AND NOT WHERE IT COULD. The entry says IsRevoked is 'a constant false' because nothing publishes. True, and incomplete: signal_rpc.go and authorize.go each MINT a token one line above the check, so a fresh UUIDv7 can never be in the filter and both would stay constant-false even with revocation fully wired. Meanwhile checkpointAuthorizer - the ONLY path where a token crosses a trust boundary, arriving from another node and unlocking a running process's entire address space - did not consult the filter at all. Fixed: the checkpoint boundary now refuses revoked tokens, checked before subject binding, and the two inert checks are removed with comments recording why a check there would be theatre. Revert-proved: deleting the check makes a revoked token authorize a checkpoint fetch. (2) THE FILTER COULD NOT FORGET, AND THE MISSING PRODUCER WAS MASKING IT. Revocations was set-only-grows with no rotation, expiry or reset. That was harmless only because nothing ever revoked - an empty filter has a 0% false-positive rate forever - so wiring a producer is precisely what would have started filling it. At 2000 entries the filter refuses 15% of VALID tokens and at 4000 more than half. The existing sizing comment even justified the geometry by saying revoked ids 'age out of relevance', describing aging that was never implemented. Fixed: a generational filter, two generations rotating at TTLMax, so an entry lives one to two periods and never less than the longest token TTL. NewRevocationsWithPeriod enforces that floor in code rather than documenting it. Rotation runs on the READ path too, or a quiet node keeps refusing tokens revoked hours ago. Revert-proved twice and attributed: a single generation fails the correctness floor with 'entry dropped before one full period elapsed'; write-only rotation fails three tests including the read-path one. (3) THE DESIGNED GOSSIP COULD NEVER HAVE FIT ITS TRANSPORT. Snapshot is fixed-width at 1024 bytes and the Serf user-event limit is 512, so broadcasting the filter would have failed checkSerfEventSize unconditionally - even with zero revocations. That is plausibly why the send half was never written: it was not forgotten, it was impossible. The entry's own phrase 'a gossip-merged revocation Bloom filter' is what steered the implementation onto Serf, and nobody checked whether the bytes fit. Fixed by broadcasting the DELTA: a 16-byte token id over PublishCluster, applied by every receiver with the same Revoke call, so merge order stays irrelevant. Triggered when a migration terminates - on FAILURE especially, since a rolled-back or stranded migration is exactly when a token is loose with no completion to bound it. Sized against a stated rate rather than a guess: the geometry sustains ~2.8 revocations/sec under 1% false positives, and Stats().RatePerSecond reports the OBSERVED rate so the assumption is checkable on a real cluster instead of trusted. (4) THE LOCATOR'S READ SIDE WAS DEAD BECAUSE ITS JOB WAS ALREADY DONE BETTER ELSEWHERE. LookupLocator had no production reader, and the obvious fix - guard the signal path on start_epoch - would have REBUILT AN EXISTING MECHANISM FROM WORSE DATA. procsig.Signal already does it: it compares the start epoch, opens a pidfd to pin the process, RECHECKS the epoch while pinned to catch recycling inside the window, and only then sends. That runs on the owning node against its own tracker - authoritative local state - where the gossiped locator is eventually consistent. So enforcement stays where it is, and LookupLocator gains the one job gossip does that Raft cannot: DIVERGENCE DETECTION. The signal path now warns when the observed locator's node disagrees with Raft's placement, naming both and the observed epoch. Diagnostic, not routing - Raft remains authoritative - and it answers the first question an operator asks when a signal goes nowhere. VERIFIED: goblin green in both resolution modes (12 packages each), the cluster suite green behind its tag, 'GOWORK=off go vet -mod=vendor -tags mage .' clean, lint 0 issues with the one pre-existing nosec in operatorkey.go untouched. RESIDUAL. (a) Delta broadcast is BEST-EFFORT. A node partitioned, restarting or joining after the event never learns of that revocation, and keeps accepting the token until it expires - bounded at TTLMax, 300s, on those nodes only. GOBLIN-DIV-057 tracks the anti-entropy that closes it, and carries the trap: Ingest fails closed by RENEWING an ingested entry, which is right for a one-shot merge and wrong for a periodic one, so the sync wire format must carry a generation. (b) Migration is the only revocation trigger. A token issued for any other verb still expires rather than being revoked. (c) Issuer retains no token-to-subject map, so 'revoke everything for instance X' remains unrepresentable; only a caller holding the token id can revoke. (d) The divergence warning is observability, not enforcement - nothing acts on it, and a persistent disagreement between gossip and Raft still needs someone reading logs.

violation: The operator key registry (GOBLIN-DIV-015 piece 1) is unforgeable through the Raft log and forgeable through a snapshot. An attacker able to append arbitrary Raft log entries can by construction act as leader on the raft-quic plane, forge an FSMSnapshot whose operator_keys map holds their own well-formed key, and install it as the cluster's root of trust on every replica in one step. Restore now validates each record's derived key id and refuses a mismatch, which makes the id-is-derived invariant hold off the Apply path too, but no check inside Restore can distinguish an honest leader's snapshot from a hostile peer's. violation: The operator key registry is authenticated by the TRANSPORT and by nothing else. Every registry guard - the empty-registry seed rule, the last-key refusal, the prev_serial replay guard, signature verification against replicated key material - runs inside FSM Apply, and InstallSnapshot does not go through Apply. FSM.Restore installs payload.GetOperatorKeys() directly and a snapshot is not a signed object, so a node holding a valid peer certificate can act as leader, forge an FSMSnapshot whose operator_keys map holds its own key, and install it as the cluster's root of trust on every replica in one step. Restore validates each record's derived key id and refuses a mismatch, which keeps the id-is-derived invariant true off the Apply path, but no check inside Restore can distinguish an honest leader's snapshot from a compromised member's - both arrive over an authenticated connection. This is the half of GOBLIN-DIV-043 that transport authentication cannot reach, and it is what still falsifies the piece-1 rationale: 'if any node in the Raft membership could empty and re-seed the registry, node compromise would become operator compromise'. Inside the membership, it does. RESOLVED 2026-08-02. The snapshot now carries the registry's PROVENANCE - the founding OperatorKeySeed and every signed OperatorKeyChange that actually mutated the registry, in apply order - and core/consensus/fsm_snapshot_trust.go replays it on Restore against the keys THIS NODE was configured with via --operator-key. A forger cannot produce the signatures, so it cannot produce a chain that replays; and the replay's output is compared against the registry the snapshot claims, so an honest chain cannot be pasted onto a dishonest result. TWO OPERATOR DECISIONS shaped it, both 2026-08-02. (1) THE ANCHOR IS SET EQUALITY, not intersection. The seed is unsigned - it must be, since it is authorized by the registry being empty and there is no key yet to sign against - which makes it the one link a forger writes freely. Anchoring on 'some key I trust appears in the chain' accepts a forged seed of {honest key, attacker key}: internally consistent, trivially valid, fatal. That is not a theoretical objection; it is a test case, and weakening the anchor makes exactly that case pass and no other. The consequence is that --operator-key now names the cluster's FOUNDING seed, immutable for the cluster's life: the registry rotates freely above it, but a node joining after a rotation is configured with the founding keys, not the current ones. (2) A NODE WITH NO CONFIGURED KEYS REFUSES a non-empty registry rather than adopting one unverified. Only mixed configuration breaks - a cluster where nobody configured a key keeps an empty registry, carries no provenance, and restores exactly as before, which is the documented fail-closed mode. Permissiveness here would have meant an attacker simply targets an unconfigured follower, and the entry could then only narrow, never close. ONE PREDICTED COST DID NOT MATERIALIZE: the entry expected a schema-reset label, but the two new fields are ADDITIVE and buf breaking passes unchanged. exit: The selection mechanism is the exit, not the start loop. Systemd-like targets: an agent is boot-local if it is WantedBy a target on the boot path and cluster-schedulable if it is not, so the distinction falls out of the dependency graph instead of being a classification someone invents. wanted_by is ALREADY parsed by the kernel's discovery and consumed by nothing, which is the shape to fix rather than repeat. Note the cost before starting: this is a design cycle, not a patch. The kernel's toposort already implements the two-relation semantics a target engine needs (hard edges order and cycle-reject; soft edges order when satisfiable and drop rather than block when they would cycle) but it lives in the kernel's internal/ tree, so the orchestrator cannot import it - the exported alternative takes an agent map, the wrong type for targets. Making it reachable is a kernel change. Closing requires a test in which one agent starts at boot and another, identical but for its target membership, does not - demonstrated by flipping the membership and showing the assertion fail. Explicitly NOT an exit: calling StartAll unfiltered, which satisfies the doc sentence and ships duplicate execution; and documenting the gap, since this entry IS that documentation. Deliberately NOT done in the change that split the supervisor: a target model MOVES Phase 2 rather than filtering it - the gate becomes a target reached and cluster join becomes a target - so building it against the current shape would put it exactly where targets restructure, which is GOBLIN-DIV-046's own argument one level up. CLOSED 2026-08-02 on internal/supervisor/targets_test.go under 'Full Build and Test'. FOUR TARGETS, named for what is TRUE when each is reached rather than for their phase number, because that is what an agent author reasons about: local.target (Phase 2), network-ready.target (Phase 3), cluster.target (Phase 4), distributed.target (Phase 5). The .target suffix follows the convention agent units already use - discovery keys off *.py.service, *.go.service, *.py.timer - and it earns its keep: an unknown bare name in wanted_by is a typo and an unknown X.target is a missing target, a distinction that did not exist when every unknown name was silently ignored. warnUnreachableTargets reports the latter, because an agent that is discovered, registered, enabled and simply never started is otherwise indistinguishable from one deliberately left schedulable. THE MODEL MOVES PHASE 2 RATHER THAN FILTERING IT, as the entry required: each phase does its work and then reaches its target, so 'start local agents' is distributed across the boot path instead of sitting at one point in it, and the Phase 3 gate finally has a producer. ONE JUDGEMENT CALL, recorded because it is a deliberate divergence from systemd: selection closes transitively over REQUIRES but NOT over WANTS. The closure over Requires is not optional - the kernel's sort ignores edges naming agents outside the map it is given, so without it a boot agent starts without a hard dependency and nothing says so. Refusing to close over Wants is the conservative half: a soft edge recruiting a cluster-schedulable template into a boot target is exactly the duplicate execution this mechanism exists to prevent. Widening later is additive; narrowing after agents rely on it would not be. DEMONSTRATED BY FAILURE, twice, both restored byte-identical. Flipping the membership - the exit's own words - makes local.target select both agents and fails the assertion. Replacing selection with an unfiltered pull, which is the StartAll this entry explicitly rejects as an exit, fails it too along with the Wants test. VERIFIED under go.work and GOWORK=off -mod=vendor, plus -tags cluster (45.8s green) and mage lint clean. The cluster run is the one that matters for the entry's measured blast radius: the sleeper fixture names no target, so it stayed a scheduling template on every node rather than also running as a boot-local process. RESIDUALS. (1) A target is reached UNCONDITIONALLY once its phase completes; there is no notion of a target FAILING because its agents did not start. A start failure is logged and the boot continues, which is deliberate - one broken node-local agent must not refuse the cluster join an operator needs in order to fix it - but it means 'target reached' asserts the phase happened, not that its agents are healthy. (2) Targets are not units: nothing can declare Requires on local.target, only WantedBy. Making anchors first-class is the remaining half of the target model. (3) Teardown is unchanged and still asymmetric - goblin stops agents through the kernel's SystemShutdown without reaching targets in reverse.

violation: Phase-aware ALPN admission does not exist. goblin-architecture.md states that connections negotiating a cluster ALPN (serf-quic, raft-quic, goblin-rpc) BEFORE Phase 4 are refused at accept with a cluster-not-ready close - 'fail closed, not fail silent, consistent with the ErrClusterNotReady model' - and that only gapi-quic is served before the cluster is up. Neither half holds. The serf and raft planes register during Phase 4 and the rpc, gapi and checkpoint planes all register together in Phase 5, so there is no window in which gapi-quic is served alone and no ALPN is ever refused on phase grounds. An unregistered ALPN is refused with CodeALPNNotServing, which is a different mechanism with a different meaning: it says nothing is listening, not that the cluster is not ready. The doc's 'listener is created early (Phase 1)' half IS now true - phase_local.go binds it - which is what makes the remaining gap precise rather than general. TestSharedListener_AdmitsRaftPeerWithIssuedCert failed at 30.01s, mtls_raft_test.go:257, 'a peer with a CA-issued client certificate never reached the raft plane', immediately preceded by: WARN refusing connection: ALPN not serving alpn=raft-quic. THIS RETIRES 'MECHANISM UNKNOWN' FOR THE MAIN FLAKE. entries/2026-08-02-the-flake-that-was-the-harness records three timing-sensitive failures on main across two of three merges with no mechanism and an explicitly REFUTED contention hypothesis. Two of those three are now confirmed to be this entry: TestSharedListener_Admits is the test that just failed here with the ALPN-not-serving line, and cluster-criu-migration is run 30740511720 above. The third, TestBootstrapExpect_Holds, has NOT had its signature compared and is not claimed - saying 'two of three, one unchecked' is the honest form, and the unchecked one is a five-minute log read for whoever opens this entry. WHAT TO DO WITH IT: the fix this entry already describes - phase-aware admission that distinguishes 'not ready yet' from 'nothing is listening' - is also the fix for the flake, because a retryable not-yet is exactly what both a joining peer and a dialing test need. Closing this entry should therefore close the flake, and the exit should say so, so that nobody later reads a green suite as evidence the flake was separately fixed. RESOLVED 2026-08-02, and the mechanism was confirmed before it was fixed: see the three occurrences recorded above. THE MEASUREMENT THAT SHAPED THE FIX, because the obvious implementation is wrong: the refusal DOES NOT ARRIVE ON THE DIAL. The listener completes the QUIC handshake, inspects the negotiated ALPN, and only then closes, so quic.DialAddr returns a LIVE CONNECTION AND A NIL ERROR and the application code lands on that connection's context a moment later. Measured on loopback: DialAddr returned in 3.08ms, the close landed 0.34ms after. A retry that inspects only the dial's error therefore retries nothing - and, worse, its test passes, because the dial 'succeeded'. That happened here: the first version of the retry test went green in 10ms against a connection that was about to be closed, and only the elapsed time gave it away.
rule: goblin-architecture.md (phase-aware admission; ErrClusterNotReady model); cooperative-ecosystem-manifesto (fail closed at boundaries)
exit: Either implement phase-aware admission or retire the claim, and the choice is not free: the gapi plane's handler needs the distributed event bus and membership, both Phase 4 objects, so serving gapi-quic before cluster join is a redesign of what that handler depends on rather than a reordering. If implemented, closing requires a test that dials a cluster ALPN before Phase 4 and asserts a cluster-not-ready close distinguishable from CodeALPNNotServing, demonstrated by removing the phase check and showing the test see the wrong code. If retired, the architecture doc's phase-aware-admission paragraph and its ALPN availability column come out in the same change, and this entry closes on the doc no longer making the claim. Do not close by narrowing the claim in prose while the behaviour is unchanged. EXIT EXTENDED 2026-08-02 (operator decision) AND CLOSED THE SAME DAY. The exit as written required only that the listener send a distinguishable code. That is satisfiable without fixing anything: NOTHING in the tree inspected the QUIC application error, so a renamed refusal would have been renamed silence and this entry would have closed beside a suite that still flaked - the close-on-the-gate failure in its purest form. So the exit gained a second clause: a joiner that meets a not-ready refusal must retry and succeed. IMPLEMENTED IN TWO HALVES. (1) core/transport/listener.go: CodeClusterNotReady (0x102) is sent when a CLUSTER ALPN arrives with no adapter and the node has not finished registering its planes; CodeALPNNotServing (0x100) now means only 'never'. The readiness signal is a PREDICATE supplied at construction, not a flag set afterwards - the listener starts accepting in Phase 1, so a value assigned later would be read before it existed, and a nil predicate is refused rather than defaulted because either default is wrong somewhere. It is set after PHASE 5, not Phase 4: serf-quic and raft-quic register in Phase 4 but goblin-rpc registers in Phase 5, so a flag set at the end of Phase 4 would tell a peer dialling rpc 'never' during the window it should hear 'not yet'. (2) core/transport/dial_retry.go: both dial sites retry while the peer answers not-ready, watching the connection's context for the post-handshake close. gapi-quic is deliberately NOT a cluster ALPN - serving it earlier is a redesign of what its handler depends on, so promising 'not yet' would promise something waiting does not deliver. DEMONSTRATED BY FAILURE, twice and independently, both restored byte-identical: removing the phase check makes the listener send CodeALPNNotServing and fails only the admission tests; removing the retry keeps the correct code and fails only the wait assertion, returning in 2.6ms instead of waiting out the peer. RESIDUALS. (1) THE PROBE IS TIME-BOUNDED, and this is the weakest part. Because the refusal arrives after the handshake, the dial watches the new connection for 50ms before trusting it - about 150x the measured 0.34ms gap, but a bound rather than a proof. A refusal slower than that yields a doomed connection, which is exactly today's behaviour and no worse, but it is not eliminated. (2) That probe costs 50ms on the HAPPY path, once per new peer connection; both callers cache per peer, so it is not per message. (3) The flake's ABSENCE cannot be proven by this change - only its mechanism was proven present. Three consecutive local cluster runs passed after the fix, which is weak evidence against an intermittent failure; the honest statement is that the cause is removed by construction and the rate should be watched. (4) DOC DIVERGENCE NOTICED IN PASSING, not fixed here: goblin-architecture.md's ALPN table lists goblin-rpc as available at 'cluster up (Phase 4)' while the code registers it in Phase 5. The implementation follows the code, not the table.
